endorsements.quote: Furthermore, the respective educational, socioeconomic and cultural background of individual patients and their families has to be considered when, for example, physicians explain PRSs ( Slunecka et al., 2021 ).
Increasing the robustness of the detected effects across different populations would go some way towards separating true causal effects from spurious associations.

unlisted_practices: Adopt interactive and participatory engagement practices between clinicians and patients for AI-driven polygenic risk scores, avoiding deficit models of communication.
Establish internationally standardised regulatory frameworks for AI-driven polygenic risk scores as medical devices that respond to fast-evolving science.
Involve research ethics committees and clinical ethics committees in the translation and implementation of AI-driven polygenic risk scores.
Embed ethics proactively, including embedded ethics approaches, throughout the research and implementation of AI-driven polygenic risk scores.
Provide education and training on AI literacy, risk interpretation, genomics and ethics to all stakeholders involved in AI-driven polygenic risk scores.
Share AI models for genetic risk prediction openly, including model weights, source code and meta diagrams, to enhance transparency.
Develop standards for communicating the uncertainty of AI-generated polygenic risk score predictions in a structured, transparent and responsible way.
Require public sharing of GWAS summary statistics in standardised formats to avoid exacerbating health inequalities.
Establish standards of fairness to reduce disparities caused by machine learning bias in genetic risk prediction.

screen.reason: This is a commentary/brief-report discussing ethical complexities and recommending proactive approaches to governance and ethical implementation of AI-driven polygenic risk scores.
